title: India Eyes Venezuelan Oil Fields as Caracas Becomes Its Fourth-Largest Crude Supplier
excerpt: Petroleum minister tells Caracas that Indian companies want upstream exploration. Imports surged 51 percent in a single month as the Hormuz crisis forces a historic rewrite of India's oil map.
body:
India's petroleum minister Hardeep Singh Puri told Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodriguez on Thursday that Indian energy companies are ready to expand into Venezuelan oil fields — a statement that would have been unthinkable a year ago, and one that captures just how dramatically the Strait of Hormuz crisis has redrawn India's energy map.

Venezuela has become India's fourth-largest crude oil supplier, up from a marginal source just months earlier. Indian refiners imported 427,000 barrels per day of Venezuelan crude in May, a 51 percent surge from 283,000 bpd in April, according to Kpler ship-tracking data cited by Reuters. India is now the second-largest buyer of Venezuelan oil after the United States, which eased sanctions on Venezuelan crude in February.

"We are working with a government that is friendly, that wants a partnership with India," an Indian foreign ministry official told Reuters. "Venezuela has traditionally been a close friend. We have collaborated very closely at the international level, so we are just going back to normal."

The meeting between Puri and Rodriguez — which included discussions with Indian energy industry executives — is focused not on spot purchases but on long-term supply arrangements, upstream exploration, production partnerships, and infrastructure development. For Venezuela, which exported 1.25 million barrels per day in May (a 61 percent jump over May 2025), India represents a stable, high-volume buyer that can help revive an oil sector battered by years of sanctions and underinvestment.

## The Hormuz Factor

The speed of this pivot has a single cause: the Strait of Hormuz, through which 45 percent of India's crude oil, half its LNG, and 90 percent of its LPG imports flowed before the US-Iran war began in March. Three months later, that chokepoint remains effectively blocked. Iran has continued launching drones and missiles at shipping, with the latest exchange this weekend involving strikes on US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain and American retaliation against Iranian coastal radar sites.

The result is an energy market under extraordinary stress. OPEC crude production has fallen to a 37-year low — just 16.33 million barrels per day in May, down 1.22 million bpd, with Iran accounting for more than half of the decline. Saudi Arabia's output dropped to levels not seen since the 1990 Gulf War. India's crude basket, which sat at $69 per barrel before the crisis, has surged past $114.

OPEC+ is expected to approve a fourth consecutive monthly increase in output quotas on Sunday, adding 188,000 bpd from July. But the hike is largely symbolic — the group's actual production has collapsed from 42.77 million bpd in February to 33.19 million in April because Gulf members simply cannot ship their oil.

## A New Oil Map

India has responded by executing the most aggressive supply diversification in its history. The country has rerouted roughly 70 percent of its crude imports away from the Strait of Hormuz, up from 55 percent before the conflict, according to an Atlantic Council analysis.

The new sourcing geography spans four continents. Russia remains India's largest alternative supplier at approximately 1.9 million bpd, though US sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil have pushed Russian oil's share of Indian imports below 20 percent, down from a peak above 33 percent. Washington's sanctions waiver for Russian crude, extended on a rolling monthly basis, currently runs through mid-June — and its renewal is uncertain.

Brazil has emerged as another critical source. Indian imports of Brazilian crude averaged 238,000 bpd in early 2026, more than double the 100,000 bpd of 2025. Asian imports of Brazilian oil overall surged to 1.8 million bpd between January and May, up from 1.2 million last year. Brazil's medium-sweet grades from its Tupi and Buzios offshore fields are well-suited for Indian refineries, though analysts caution that Brazilian production can only grow by 50,000 to 100,000 bpd in the short term.

Africa's export majors, Nigeria and Angola, have also seen increased Indian purchasing.

## The Vulnerability Underneath

For all the scale of this pivot, India remains deeply exposed. The world's third-largest oil importer depends on foreign crude for 85 percent of domestic demand. The International Energy Agency estimates India's strategic petroleum reserves cover just seven days of consumption — far short of the 90-day benchmark that the IEA recommends.

A 2020 US-India memorandum on strategic reserves has never been implemented. The Atlantic Council argues that operationalising it, along with expanding port infrastructure at Mundra (which launched India's first terminal for very large crude carriers in January 2026) and signing long-term US LNG and LPG contracts, would give India durable supply chain resilience rather than the current dependence on temporary sanctions waivers.

JPMorgan predicts the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in June, with Brent crude remaining near $100 per barrel for most of the year. If the strait stays closed, however, each additional month adds roughly $5 per barrel to the bank's third-quarter oil price forecast and $15 to its fourth-quarter estimate.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian families at home and abroad, the arithmetic is direct. Higher crude prices feed through to petrol, diesel, and cooking gas bills within weeks. The rupee, already under pressure, faces further depreciation risk if import costs keep climbing. Remittances from the Gulf — where an estimated 8.5 million Indians live and work, some in countries now absorbing Iranian missile strikes — buy less when denominated in a weakening currency.

The broader structural shift may carry a silver lining. India's willingness to invest in Venezuelan upstream assets, diversify to Brazilian and African crude, and build VLCC-capable port infrastructure signals a government that has absorbed the lesson of Hormuz: that energy security cannot rest on a single maritime corridor, no matter how convenient the geography once was.

Puri's meeting with Rodriguez was not just about buying more oil. It was about ensuring India never again finds itself this vulnerable.
